title: Spalding Symposium on Indian Religions extends its 2027 call for papers to 20 November
dek: The 52nd symposium meets in Cambridge from 2 to 4 April 2027 on the theme of making, mapping and maintaining the world. Proposals are now due by 20 November 2026.
body: The organisers of the Spalding Symposium on Indian Religions have moved the deadline for paper proposals for their 2027 meeting from 15 November to 20 November 2026. The 52nd symposium will be held in person at Selwyn College and the Faculty of Divinity, University of Cambridge, from Friday 2 to Sunday 4 April 2027.

The theme is 'Making, Mapping, and Maintaining the World'. The call invites work on how worlds are brought into being, for example through creation narratives, ritual, consecration of images or the forming of canons; how they are ordered and located, through sacred geography, pilgrimage, cosmological diagrams, lineages and the categories used to classify traditions; and how they are kept going, through dharma and law, temple governance, ritual calendars, the care of manuscripts and the stewardship of communities and environments. Papers may come from the humanities, social sciences or other disciplines and use textual, ethnographic, visual, material or digital methods.
The two keynote speakers, announced with the extension on 9 and 10 November, are Professor Nina Mirnig of the University of Vienna and Professor Peter Flügel of SOAS University of London.

Proposals are sent through an online form and need a title, an abstract of up to 500 words, a short biography and an affiliation. Main papers have 30 minutes plus 15 for discussion; a graduate panel for advanced doctoral candidates has 20 minutes plus 10. A conference fee applies; the organisers hope to cover some presenters' costs, and doctoral students whose papers are accepted may be eligible for bursaries. Results are due in early December, and individual feedback will not be given.
The local convenor is Dr Chris Jones of Cambridge, working with Kush Depala (Heidelberg), Dr Hershini Soneji (Cambridge) and Dr Saran Suebsantiwongse (Leiden).
place: Selwyn College and Faculty of Divinity, University of Cambridge, UK
